strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: no prior real-world dataset exists for camera-based Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) from aerial/UAV viewpoints, whereas SSC is well-studied for autonomous driving.

Proposes a genuinely novel, LiDAR-free data-generation framework that uses SfM+MVS reconstruction plus multi-view 2D-to-3D label lifting, class-aware instance densification (silhouette-based voxel carving), and ground-surface reconstruction (Poisson) to produce dense volumetric semantic ground truth while manually annotating <10% of images (<7% by supplementary Table 8) -- a scalable and practically important contribution for future dataset creation on other UAV platforms.

Dataset scale is respectable for a first-of-its-kind resource: 9 scenes, >20k samples, ~194,000 m^2 coverage, 3 altitudes, 4 seasons, 22 semantic classes, and paired metric depth maps (also releasing a fine-tuned Depth-Anything-V2 model).

Careful, quantitatively grounded validation of data quality: reprojection error (~1.24 px average), image overlap statistics (>90%), scene-wise depth histograms, and comparisons against both terrestrial (SemanticKITTI, Occ3D, etc.) and aerial 2D segmentation benchmarks in terms of scale and class taxonomy.

Benchmarking of a recent state-of-the-art SSC method (CGFormer) and a metric depth model (DAv2) on the new benchmark yields informative findings (e.g., strong class-frequency correlation, altitude-dependent depth degradation, performance gap versus terrestrial domains) that motivate future aerial-specific SSC research.

Extensive and transparent supplementary material (implementation details, per-scene reprojection error, annotation ratios, DBSCAN parameters, class-wise IoU tables, additional qualitative visualizations) supports reproducibility and rigor beyond the main paper.
weaknesses: The benchmark is built from only 9 scenes collected in a single, undisclosed geographic region; despite the large sample/voxel counts, true scene diversity (terrain types, architectural styles, vegetation, climates) is limited compared to multi-city/multi-region terrestrial datasets, which may constrain generalizability claims.

Ground-truth quality rests entirely on the accuracy of the camera-based SfM+MVS reconstruction and subsequent label-lifting/densification pipeline; only indirect proxies (reprojection RMSE, qualitative visualizations) are provided to validate this pipeline -- there is no independent accuracy check (e.g., against LiDAR or held-out manual 3D annotation) quantifying point-cloud/label correctness, semantic label-transfer accuracy, or the effect of majority-vote/kNN label propagation on boundary regions.

The framework explicitly assumes static scenes, which is a material limitation for realistic UAV/urban settings with moving vehicles, pedestrians, etc.; this restricts the benchmark's applicability to dynamic real-world deployment scenarios, and is only listed as future work rather than addressed.

Severe class imbalance (e.g., "Building" alone ~76% of instance points; several classes near 0% in the supplementary frequency table) may make several of the 22 classes essentially unevaluable, which somewhat undercuts the claimed benefit of a fine-grained taxonomy.

Only a single downstream SSC model (CGFormer) and a single depth model (DAv2) are benchmarked; broader method coverage (e.g., additional recent voxel/BEV/TPV-based SSC approaches cited in Related Work) would better establish the benchmark's discriminative value across architectures.

No inter-annotator agreement or annotation-quality analysis is reported for the manually labeled 2D masks that seed the whole pipeline, despite their central role in determining the reliability of all propagated 3D labels.

Reported SSC benchmark numbers (mIoU around 0.24-0.26 in Table 11) are quite low; while partly framed as evidence of dataset difficulty/domain gap, this also leaves open the possibility that a nontrivial portion of the low performance stems from label/geometry noise in the automatically generated ground truth rather than purely from genuine scene complexity, and the paper does not fully disentangle these factors.

strengths: Introduces what appears to be the first real-world, camera-only aerial Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) benchmark, addressing a genuine gap: prior SSC datasets are LiDAR-based and terrestrial, while aerial UAV platforms often cannot carry LiDAR due to mass/energy/regulatory constraints.

The data-generation pipeline is technically well described (SfM+MVS reconstruction, 2D-to-3D label lifting via multi-view correspondence, class-aware densification with instance-level voxel carving and Poisson surface reconstruction for ground classes, frustum-culled per-frame ground truth with invalid/surface/occluded masks). The formalism in Sec. 3 is precise and appears reproducible in principle.

Reasonable scale/diversity along some axes: 9 scenes, >20,000 samples, 3 altitudes (30/40/50m), 4 seasons, urban/industrial/rural scenarios, 22 semantic classes, with quantitative comparison to existing terrestrial and aerial 2D datasets (Tables 2-3).
Low manual annotation burden is demonstrated (sub-10% of images annotated per scene while covering >99% of reconstructed points), which is a useful practical efficiency claim supported by numbers.

Includes metric depth map benchmarking (fine-tuned Depth-Anything-V2) and SSC benchmarking (CGFormer) with class-, group-, and altitude-wise breakdowns, plus an interesting cross-domain (aerial vs. driving) zero-shot generalization experiment for monocular depth in the supplementary.

Supplementary material provides useful transparency: reprojection error per scene, DBSCAN parameters, annotation ratios, image overlap statistics, and depth histograms, which aids reproducibility assessment.
weaknesses: Despite being framed as 'a comprehensive 3D aerial vision benchmark,' the actual benchmarking is very narrow: only a single SSC method (CGFormer) and a single depth model (DAv2) are evaluated. No comparison across multiple SSC architectures (e.g., VoxFormer, TPVFormer, SGN, MonoScene) is provided, which is standard practice for benchmark papers and essential to support claims of exposing 'challenges specific to elevated viewpoints' rather than idiosyncrasies of one model.

The dataset itself is small in scene diversity: only 9 scenes total, split into 5 train / 2 val / 2 test, all collected within 'a single geographic region' (locations withheld for review). This raises concerns about the generalizability of conclusions drawn from the benchmark and about geographic/architectural diversity of the ground-truth labels.

Semantic ground truth is derived from a largely automated pipeline (majority voting across multi-view correspondences, kNN propagation to unlabeled points, DBSCAN-based instance extraction, Poisson reconstruction for ground classes) but no explicit quantitative validation of label quality/noise (e.g., agreement with independently fully-annotated regions, inter-annotator consistency, or ablation on kNN/DBSCAN parameter sensitivity) is reported beyond geometric reprojection error, which does not measure semantic correctness.

The framework explicitly assumes static scenes and excludes dynamic objects, a significant limitation for an aerial/UAV benchmark intended to support downstream robotics applications where dynamic agents (vehicles, pedestrians) are often of primary interest; this is acknowledged only as future work.

Reported SSC performance is very low across the board (mIoU values in the single digits/low tens per Table 11), and while the paper frames this as revealing domain gap, with only one baseline evaluated it is unclear whether this reflects genuine SSC difficulty in the aerial domain or specific unsuitability/under-adaptation of CGFormer to this setup (e.g., depth backbone swap, grid resolution change from 256×256×32 to 192×128×128).

Class distribution is extremely imbalanced (e.g., Building 75.7%, several instance classes <0.01%, per supplementary Table 6), and the paper does not discuss how this affects the reliability or fairness of the benchmark's class-wise/mIoU evaluation protocol for rare classes.

Reproducibility is constrained in the current submission: exact scene locations are withheld, and full dataset/code release is conditioned on acceptance ('Upon acceptance, we will release...'), making independent verification of the dataset itself currently impossible for reviewers beyond the reported statistics and figures.

strengths: Introduces the first real-world, camera-based aerial Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) benchmark, filling a clear gap since prior SSC datasets target ground-vehicle/terrestrial scenarios.

Proposes a LiDAR-free, scalable data-generation pipeline (SfM+MVS reconstruction, sparse 2D manual annotation lifted to dense 3D via multi-view correspondences, class-aware densification/voxelization) that reduces manual 3D annotation effort to <10% of images while achieving high 2D-to-3D label coverage (>99% of points).

Comprehensive dataset scale and diversity: 9 scenes, >20,000 samples, 22 semantic classes, 3 altitudes, 4 seasons, and ~194,000 m^2 coverage, with clear comparison tables against existing terrestrial and 2D aerial benchmarks (Tables 2-3).

Thorough supporting evidence for data quality: low SfM/MVS reprojection error (1.24 px average), high image overlap (>90%) statistics, per-scene annotation ratios, class-wise DBSCAN parameters, and extensive qualitative visualizations (point clouds, voxel grids, annotation masks) in the main paper and supplementary.

Useful benchmark experiments beyond dataset release: evaluates a state-of-the-art SSC method (CGFormer) with altitude-, class-, and group-wise breakdowns, and trains/releases a metric monocular depth model (DAv2-OccuFly) with cross-domain (terrestrial vs. aerial) generalization experiments, providing actionable insights (e.g., altitude affects metric depth accuracy; existing SSC methods underperform on aerial data due to class imbalance).
Honest discussion of limitations (static-scene assumption, temporal inconsistency across altitude flights, semi-manual labeling) and reasonable directions for future automation.
weaknesses: Only a single SSC method (CGFormer) is benchmarked; no comparison across multiple representative SSC architectures (e.g., VoxFormer, TPVFormer, MonoScene) is provided, limiting the demonstrated breadth of the benchmark's utility for method comparison.

The pseudo-ground-truth generation pipeline is validated mainly via reprojection error and coverage ratio, but there is no direct quantitative accuracy check of the final lifted 3D semantic labels against any independently verified ground truth (e.g., held-out fully manual 3D annotation), so the fidelity of the automatically propagated 3D labels is only indirectly supported.

Test split is small (2 scenes, 3,842 samples) relative to the overall dataset, which may limit the statistical robustness of the reported benchmark numbers and class-wise breakdowns, especially for rare classes.

Severe class imbalance (Building alone accounts for ~75.7% of voxels per Table 6) is acknowledged as affecting model performance but is not otherwise mitigated or analyzed for its impact on the reliability/interpretability of the mIoU metrics.

The dataset is collected from a single (currently undisclosed) geographic region across 9 scenes, which may limit generalizability claims despite the diversity in scenario type/altitude/season; geographic diversity is inherently constrained.

The framework explicitly assumes static scenes, excluding dynamic objects/behaviors that are often relevant for downstream aerial robotics applications, and this is a non-trivial scope limitation rather than a purely presentational issue.

strengths: First real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark, addressing a genuine gap since prior SSC work focuses on ground/autonomous-driving domains and prior aerial 3D datasets rely on LiDAR or synthetic data.

Novel, scalable, LiDAR-free data generation framework (SfM+MVS reconstruction, sparse 2D annotation lifted to 3D via multi-view correspondence, class-aware instance/ground/other densification and voxelization, frustum-culled per-frame ground truth with surface/occluded/invalid masks) that reduces manual 3D annotation effort to <10% of images while covering >99% of points, which is a meaningful engineering and methodological contribution beyond just a dataset release.

Reasonably large and diverse dataset: 9 scenes, >20k samples, 21 semantic classes, 3 altitudes, 4 seasons, ~194,000 m^2, with matched RGB, semantic voxel grids, and metric depth maps, substantially exceeding prior aerial depth datasets (WildUAV, UseGeo) and comparable/larger than SemanticKITTI in several respects.

Careful validation of the data pipeline itself: reprojection error analysis (1.24 px average), manual spot-check against 135 independently annotated frames (92% pixel-wise agreement), and comparison of annotation efficiency versus pseudo-labeling (SAM-based) baselines showing manual lifting is necessary for quality.

Benchmarking of state-of-the-art terrestrial SSC methods (Symphonies, DISC) and depth foundation models (MapAnything, Metric3Dv2, DepthAnythingV2/V3) on OccuFly, with both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings, revealing a clear and useful domain gap that motivates the benchmark's value; altitude-wise and class-wise breakdowns in supplementary add depth to the analysis.

Thorough supplementary material with implementation details, hyperparameters (DBSCAN, Poisson reconstruction, kNN), per-scene statistics, qualitative visualizations across all 9 scenes, and additional evaluation tables, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is still modest at the scene level: only 9 scenes (6 train, 2 val, 2 test... actually 5 train/2 val/2 test based on Table 1), all collected within a single geographic region (Ingolstadt, Germany), which limits geographic/architectural diversity and generalizability claims despite large sample counts derived from repeated frames of the same few scenes.

The semantic annotation pipeline still requires substantial manual 2D labeling (some scenes ~29 minutes/image, up to 17% of images annotated) and the paper's own experiment shows automated pseudo-labeling (SAM-based) is inadequate (17.58% mIoU), so the framework's scalability claims are somewhat overstated for very large-scale future extension.

Static-scene assumption explicitly acknowledged as a limitation: dynamic objects are not handled, which may reduce fidelity in real-world deployment scenarios (e.g., traffic, moving people) relevant to UAV applications like surveillance.

No new SSC or depth model is proposed; the benchmark exposes that existing methods perform poorly (mIoU as low as ~2%), but the paper does not provide any baseline adaptation, domain adaptation strategy, or architecture modification to close this gap, which somewhat limits the immediate actionable contribution beyond highlighting the problem.

Depth ground truth is derived from the same SfM+MVS reconstruction used for semantic labels, so metric depth maps and occupancy grids are not independent modalities—errors in reconstruction (526% scale deviation reported for DepthAnything3 zero-shot, and depth map noise) could propagate to both label sources, and reliance on RTK/GNSS pose accuracy is not deeply analyzed for potential systematic bias.

The class taxonomy, while described as fine-grained (21 classes), shows heavily skewed frequency distribution (Building 62%, many classes <1%), which the paper acknowledges causes near-zero detection for rare classes in benchmarks; this imbalance is not deeply discussed as a limitation for benchmark design (e.g., no rebalancing or class-weighted analysis besides raw mIoU reporting).

Presentation could be improved: notation in Sec 3.3 is dense and some equations (e.g., masks, ground-truth sampling) are somewhat terse, potentially hindering reproducibility for readers without careful cross-referencing to supplementary; also minor consistency issues (e.g., train split scene count wording vs table).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem (aerial/UAV camera-based semantic scene completion), for which essentially no camera-only real-world dataset currently exists.

The LiDAR-free data-generation pipeline (SfM+MVS reconstruction, sparse 2D annotation lifted to dense 3D points via multi-view correspondences, class-aware densification/voxelization, frustum-culled per-frame GT sampling) is described with careful mathematical formalism and is a reasonable engineering solution to the lack of aerial LiDAR.

Reasonably thorough supplementary material: reprojection-error analysis, annotation-efficiency statistics, class-frequency tables, per-scene visualizations, and altitude/class-wise breakdowns support some of the paper's efficiency and fidelity claims.
Benchmarks both SSC and monocular metric depth estimation, exposing a clear and (if valid) practically important gap between terrestrial/indoor vision foundation models and aerial imagery.
weaknesses: Data diversity is very limited: all 9 scenes are captured in a single geographic region (Ingolstadt, Germany) with only two UAV platforms and a single camera model per platform, undermining the claimed 'geographic diversity' and the generality of conclusions about foundation-model failure on 'aerial data' broadly.

The dataset is extremely small at the scene level (9 scenes total, 5/2/2 train/val/test split); drawing benchmark-level conclusions and reporting per-class IoU tables from 2 test scenes is statistically fragile, especially given many rare classes (Crane, Bicycle, Cable, Rock, Person, etc.) occupy <0.01% of voxels and show 0.00% IoU for both evaluated methods, i.e., they are effectively untestable with this data.

Potential circularity in the ground-truth generation: both the semantic voxel grid and the metric depth maps are derived from the same classical SfM+MVS point cloud that is also implicitly used to judge geometric fidelity (reprojection error, 92% pixel agreement on 135 extra annotations). There is no independent, higher-accuracy reference (e.g., LiDAR or RTK-surveyed ground control) against which the reconstructed 'ground truth' geometry itself is validated, so absolute metric accuracy of the GT (not just internal consistency) remains unverified.

The reported baseline results are extremely weak (mIoU around 2% for both Symphonies and DISC across all altitudes, with most classes at or near 0%), which raises the question of whether the benchmark, as constructed, currently provides a meaningful or discriminative testbed for method development rather than simply demonstrating near-complete failure — the paper does not analyze whether this stems from genuine domain gap, GT noise/sparsity, or class imbalance.

Methodological novelty is limited: the pipeline largely composes existing off-the-shelf components (COLMAP-style SfM+MVS, DBSCAN clustering, alpha-shape silhouettes, Poisson surface reconstruction, majority-vote label fusion) without a new algorithmic contribution; the main claimed novelty is the annotation-lifting/densification recipe, which is not evaluated against alternative design choices (e.g., no ablation on the effect of the <10% annotation ratio on GT quality, no comparison against LiDAR-based GT for calibration).

Benchmarking breadth is narrow: only two SSC baselines (Symphonies, DISC) are adapted (by simply swapping the depth backbone), with no attempt to retrain/redesign a model tailored to aerial altitude-varying viewpoints, and no ablation isolating which architectural components fail; this limits the paper's usefulness as a 'benchmark' beyond reporting that existing terrestrial models transfer poorly.

Severe long-tailed class distribution (Building alone is 62% of voxels; several classes are below 0.01%) is acknowledged only descriptively; no strategy (class re-weighting, merged taxonomy, or evaluation protocol adjustment) is proposed to make the benchmark tractable for the rare classes it claims to support.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: no prior real-world, camera-based aerial SSC benchmark exists, and the paper convincingly motivates why LiDAR-based pipelines used in autonomous-driving SSC datasets are impractical for UAVs (mass/energy constraints, sparse returns from elevated viewpoints).

The proposed LiDAR-free data generation pipeline (SfM+MVS reconstruction, sparse 2D annotation lifted to 3D via multi-view correspondences, class-aware densification/voxelization, frustum-culled ground-truth sampling with surface/occluded/invalid masks) is a coherent, well-engineered contribution in its own right, not just a data dump; the formalization in Sec. 3 is detailed and largely reproducible.

Strong efficiency claim is empirically substantiated: <10% of images manually annotated recovers >99% of 3D points (Eq. 3, Table 9), and the framework is validated via reprojection error (avg 1.24 px) and an independent 135-sample manual cross-check (92% pixel agreement), giving reasonable confidence in label quality despite the absence of LiDAR ground truth.

Scale and coverage are meaningful relative to prior art: >20K samples, 21 semantic classes, 3 altitudes, 4 seasons, >193,000 m², compared quantitatively against terrestrial (Table 2) and aerial depth (Table 3) benchmarks.

Benchmarking two axes (SSC and metric monocular depth) with both zero-shot and fine-tuned foundation models is a useful contribution beyond a static dataset release, clearly demonstrating a domain gap (e.g., near-zero mIoU for SOTA SSC methods, large metric-scale deviations for depth foundation models) that motivates future aerial-specific research.

Extensive supplementary material (class taxonomy, DBSCAN parameters, per-scene reprojection errors, annotation ratios, altitude/class-wise breakdowns, image-overlap maps) supports reproducibility and transparency substantially beyond the typical benchmark paper.
weaknesses: All 9 scenes are collected within a single broader geographic region (Ingolstadt, Germany); despite covering urban/industrial/rural environments and 4 seasons, the claim of a general "aerial domain" benchmark is somewhat overstated given the limited geographic and cultural diversity (building styles, road layouts, vegetation types) compared to, e.g., multi-city terrestrial benchmarks.

The dataset's ground truth is itself generated by classical SfM+MVS reconstruction rather than an independent sensor (no LiDAR used anywhere for validation), so residual systematic errors from the reconstruction pipeline (e.g., moving objects, texture-less areas, thin structures) could propagate into the "ground truth" without being caught by reprojection-error or the small 135-sample manual spot check; a more rigorous external validation (e.g., against surveyed geometry or a LiDAR subset) would strengthen confidence.

The severe class imbalance (Building alone is 62% of voxels per Table 7, several classes under 0.01%) means aggregate mIoU/IoU numbers reported for baselines are likely dominated by a handful of classes; the paper's altitude/class-wise tables (Table 11) confirm most rare classes are essentially undetected, raising the question of whether the benchmark can meaningfully discriminate future methods on the long tail without additional class-balancing or per-class weighting strategy discussion.

Only two existing SSC methods (Symphonies, DISC) and a handful of depth foundation models are evaluated; no aerial-adapted baseline or ablation study of the authors' own densification/voxelization design choices (e.g., sensitivity to DBSCAN parameters, α-shape parameter, Poisson reconstruction depth) is provided, limiting insight into how robust the benchmark's ground truth is to these hyperparameter choices.

The framework explicitly assumes static scenes and acknowledges (in the conclusion) that dynamic objects, cross-altitude temporal inconsistencies, and manual mask annotation remain open issues; these are reasonable future-work items but do somewhat limit the completeness/scalability claims made in the abstract and introduction.

Reported baseline performance is extremely low (e.g., <2% mIoU for DISC), which, combined with the lack of any aerial-tailored model or strong baseline, leaves it unclear whether the benchmark can yet support fine-grained method comparison beyond confirming that existing terrestrial methods fail outright.
